description: We are a team of computer science students passionate about technology, space exploration, and solving real-world problems. We are interested in software development, data analysis, research, and creative problem-solving, and we are excited to learn, collaborate, and turn ideas into practical solutions using NASA’s open data.
summary:
LunarSight is an interactive planning prototype that shows how the Sun and Earth appear from a chosen point on the Moon over a chosen mission period. It was built for the NASA Space Apps 2026 challenge on lunar south pole landing site evaluation.

Problem: Near the south pole the Sun sits very low, so small changes in place or date change both sunlight and the view of Earth. Mission teams need both, but the data is spread across detailed tools that are hard to compare.

Solution: Users select a location or enter coordinates, then set a start date, duration and minimum Sun and Earth elevation. LunarSight reports Sun availability, Earth visibility and the longest time both are up together. It shows elevation charts, a sky view and timelines. Users can save scenarios, compare two side by side, and export CSV or JSON.

Data: JPL Horizons supplies Sun and Earth positions. NASA Moon Trek supplies the map layer, and LROC QuickMap supplies surface context.

Example: Over one week, 89°S has Sun 100% and Earth 0%. At 85°S, 45°E, Earth is visible 13.3% of the time (22.4 h), so the site choice changes the result.
Limits: Results are geometric. They ignore mountains and crater walls and make no claim about power, communications reliability or landing safety. The reference points are not approved landing sites.

Next step: Validate and integrate Moon Trek elevation data for terrain-aware visibility.
details:
LunarSight is an interactive website that helps users explore lunar locations and compare possible mission periods using sourced lunar imagery and Sun–Earth geometry. It addresses a planning question: how do location, timing, and mission requirements affect the conditions available on the Moon?

Users select a location on a textured 3D Moon, choose a reference or historical location, or enter coordinates manually. They then define a UTC start time, mission duration, sampling interval, observer height, and minimum Sun and Earth elevation thresholds.

The application retrieves apparent Sun and Earth positions from NASA/JPL Horizons. It calculates the percentage of the mission period meeting each elevation threshold, the longest continuous simultaneous overlap, and periods below the selected Sun threshold. Charts, visibility tracks, time playback, and a local sky view help users understand these results.

A mission-start finder compares multiple starting times for a fixed-duration mission. It ranks the sampled candidates by continuous Sun/Earth overlap, helping users investigate alternatives without repeatedly changing dates manually. Users can also save scenarios, compare results, share input settings, and export data.

LunarSight brings together three main resources:

  • LROC QuickMap: observation records, image footprints, and original product links.
  • NASA Moon Trek: lunar imagery and regional surface-context layers.
  • NASA/JPL Horizons: the ephemerides supporting our temporal calculations.

The website also includes an optional sampled solar-disk overlap tool for eclipse screening. This remains separate from the main availability calculations.

We developed the project using TypeScript, React, Vite, Three.js, Recharts, Node.js, and Express. We used Zod for input validation, Git and GitHub for collaboration, and Vercel for deployment. Automated checks use Node’s test runner and Playwright. The project requires no specialized hardware.

The creative contribution is the connection between spatial exploration and time-based comparison. Users can move from selecting a lunar point to investigating conditions, testing possible starts, comparing alternatives, and reviewing the exact source requests within one interface.

Our intended impact is to make lunar mission-planning concepts more accessible to students, educators, and space enthusiasts. LunarSight supports learning and preliminary investigation while making scientific assumptions visible.

Throughout development, our team considered usability, responsive design, source traceability, coordinate conventions, sampling resolution, service reliability, and fair scenario comparison. Matching cached Horizons responses support repeatable demonstrations, while unavailable requests produce explicit errors.

We also kept the project’s limits clear. Observer height is measured above the Horizons reference sphere, and the main calculations exclude terrain obstruction and eclipse correction. The website does not certify landing safety or predict electrical power or radio-link performance. These boundaries help users interpret the results responsibly and identify the validation needed for future development.
